name: Beacon Glacialis
geological_features: A planetary ice sheet with a mirror-smooth surface in the equatorial regions
Deep nitrogen ice glaciers flowing from the poles toward the equator
Cryotectonic ridges where ice plates converge
specific_features: The planet's mirror-smooth ice reflects stellar light so efficiently it serves as a natural navigational beacon
description: Beacon Glacialis is a medium ice world whose equatorial ice sheet has been polished by aeolian processes into a surface of mirror-like smoothness that reflects stellar light with extraordinary efficiency. The reflection is visible across the system, a steady point of light that varies predictably with the planet's rotation, effectively serving as a natural lighthouse for navigators. The polar regions are rougher, their nitrogen ice glaciers flowing equatorward in slow rivers that feed the polished zone with fresh material.

The surface smoothness is a product of the thin atmosphere's persistent winds, which carry fine ice particles that abrade any irregularity and deposit a polished layer over time. The cryotectonic ridges where ice plates converge are the only significant topographical features, their compressed forms rising a few hundred meters above the surrounding flatness before the wind and ice erosion begin to smooth them as well. The planet is engaged in a perpetual contest between tectonic forces that create features and atmospheric forces that erase them.

Beacon Glacialis has served as a navigational reference since the system was first charted, its distinctive reflection noted in the earliest survey records. The predictable variation in brightness as the planet rotates has been used to calibrate optical sensors and timing systems, and its position in the system makes it visible from nearly every significant orbital path. The natural beacon function has been supplemented but not replaced by artificial navigation aids.

The nitrogen ice glaciers represent a potentially valuable volatile resource, and small-scale extraction operations have been proposed for the rougher polar regions where landing and surface operations are feasible. The equatorial mirror zone has been left undisturbed by informal consensus — its navigational value is considered greater than any resource it might yield, and there is a widespread reluctance to mar a phenomenon that required billions of years and perfect conditions to create.
